title: The Iran Shock Is Not Over
gist: Six months after Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz in what Bordoff and O'Sullivan call the largest disruption of global energy flow in history, the feared global energy crisis has not materialized; they argue the resilience is real but not a reason for complacency, because Ukraine, the stop-start green transition and the AI buildout have already turned energy into a usable economic weapon.

insights.claim: Iran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz six months ago was the largest disruption of global energy flow in history, yet the energy crisis that markets and governments expected has not arrived.
insights.speaker: Jason Bordoff
insights.so_what: The market's demonstrated ability to absorb a total Hormuz outage argues against paying a large permanent geopolitical risk premium in crude — but it also means positioning is thin if a second shock lands.
insights.quote: It was, as Meghan O’Sullivan and Jason Bordoff pointed out in Foreign Affairs at the time, the largest disruption of global energy flow in history.
insights.locator: When Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz

insights.claim: The relative calm in energy markets in recent months is a lull rather than a resolution, and treating it as proof of durable stability is the central analytical error to avoid.
insights.speaker: Jason Bordoff
insights.so_what: Argues for keeping optionality on tail-risk energy hedges rather than fully unwinding them into the calm.
insights.quote: They warn that the relative stability of recent months cannot be cause for complacency.
insights.locator: The world’s ability to manage that disruption

insights.claim: Three forces in just the last few years — Russia's invasion of Ukraine, the fits and starts of the green transition, and the AI buildout — have jointly remade energy markets and the politics underneath them.
insights.speaker: Jason Bordoff
insights.so_what: A framework for attributing energy price and policy moves: datacenter load growth now sits alongside war and transition policy as a first-order driver of power and fuel demand.
insights.locator: But in just the last few years

insights.claim: Energy has been re-established as a devastating economic weapon, making it an instrument of national security policy rather than just a traded commodity.
insights.speaker: Jason Bordoff
insights.so_what: Implies rising state intervention in energy flows — embargoes, blockades, export controls — which raises volatility and favors owners of diversified, politically safe supply.
insights.quote: shown energy to be a devastating economic weapon
insights.locator: the AI buildout have remade energy markets

themes.theme: Watch list: China clean energy and Venezuela

insights.claim: China's dominance of clean energy and the Trump administration's Venezuela oil deal are treated as the two live fronts where the new energy order is being contested alongside the Hormuz question.
insights.speaker: Jason Bordoff
insights.so_what: Flags Venezuelan barrel re-entry and Chinese clean-tech supply chains as the specific policy variables to track for the next repricing in energy.
insights.locator: Dan Kurtz-Phelan spoke to them on Tuesday, September 8
